title: Remember a good person
hook: keep someone who lived virtuously in mind (Meditations 11.26)

segments.voice: Yesterday: four failures. Your line was four failures. Which one did you catch, and did you wipe it out? Day six hundred twenty-six.

Think of the person whose voice you hear when you're about to cut a corner. A grandmother, a coach, a teacher who believed in you. You might not have seen them in years. They might not be alive. But in certain moments they're right there beside you, and you stand up a little straighter. Marcus had an old rule for exactly that. He'd found it written down somewhere, and copied it into book eleven. Today: remember a good person.
screen: `THE VOICE AT THE CORNER.` → `YOU STAND UP STRAIGHTER.` → `REMEMBER A GOOD PERSON.`

segments.voice: First, the rule. In the writings of the Ephesians, Marcus says, there was this precept: keep constantly in mind one of the people of the past who lived with virtue. That's the whole entry. Second, a puzzle about the source. Who were these Ephesians? That's what the manuscripts say, but some editors have suggested it should read Epicureans, followers of Epicurus. There's a reason to think so. Seneca, in his eleventh letter, passes on Epicurus's advice: choose some good person and keep them always before your eyes, living as if they were watching. Scholars still debate the reading. Either way, the idea is old, and it was shared across rival schools. Third, Marcus did it himself. Book one of the Meditations is exactly this practice. It's a list of people and what he learned from each: his grandfather's good temper, his mother's generosity and simple way of living, his teachers, his adoptive father Antoninus. Before the philosophy begins, Marcus remembers good people. Fourth, why it works. A rule is abstract. A person is concrete. In a hard moment, what's right? is a big question. What would she do? often answers itself. The person you remember doesn't have to have been perfect. They only have to be good in the one way you need right now.
screen: `KEEP A GOOD PERSON IN MIND.` · `EPHESIANS, OR EPICUREANS?` · `BOOK ONE IS THIS PRACTICE.` · `WHAT WOULD SHE DO?` · then, large: `REMEMBER THEM.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Bring one good person to mind: living or gone, famous or known only to you. See their face. Hear their voice. Remember one specific thing they did, one moment that showed who they were. Let yourself feel grateful for it, and for them. Then picture a moment coming up today when you'll need them, and imagine them there with you. The bell holds the time.
Remember a good person. An old rule Marcus copied: keep in mind someone who lived with virtue, and let them stand beside you. Today's word.
Your line: remember them. At one hard moment today, ask what your good person would do. Day six hundred twenty-six.

screen: `DAY 626 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: NO THIEF OF THE WILL.`

howItsDone: Many readers of the Meditations keep a particular person in mind, a grandparent, a teacher or a figure from history, and in hard moments ask what that person would do.

options: call to mind someone who lived with virtue.
fork.reveal: keep in mind one of the people of the past who practiced virtue, says the rule he copied. Seneca credits Epicurus with similar advice: live as if a good person were watching.

original.note: Greek: virtue, excellence. the rule is to remember someone who lived with aretē.

trapdoor: what you thought: have a role model.
what it means: keep one good person in mind, so in hard moments the question becomes concrete: what would they do?
what a scholar hears: the manuscripts read Ephesians; some editors emend it to Epicureans, matching advice Seneca credits to Epicurus in Letter 11.

notes: 11.26 paraphrased (Long: 'In the writings of the Ephesians there was this precept, constantly to think of some one of the men of former times who practised virtue.'). Confirm, and confirm the Ephesians/Epicureans emendation history (often credited to Gataker).
Seneca, Letter 11: Epicurus's advice to cherish some good man and keep him always before your eyes. Confirm section numbers.
Book one details: grandfather Verus (good morals, government of temper), mother (piety, beneficence, simplicity in living), Antoninus (1.16). Confirm.
